lessonRef.unitTitle: PF3 — Budgeting and Saving: Building a Budget That Survives a Surprise
lessonRef.title: Error and misconception analysis: incentives to set aside income for future consumption

focus: incentives to set aside income for future consumption
objective: Find the error in a fictional argument that dismisses saving, recompute the figure correctly, and separate the return on savings from the savings themselves.
scenario: A fictional student wrote the argument below about a simulated savings account. The reasoning contains one specific mistake.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the fictional argument as written in these directions

tasks.directions: The fictional argument reads: "My account pays 4% a year. I can only put in $40 a month. So saving earns me 4% of $40, which is $1.60 a year. That is not worth doing." Assume interest is credited on the average balance across the year, which for level monthly deposits is about half the year-end total.

prompts.text: What figure did the fictional student compute, taking 4% of a single $40 deposit?

tasks.directions: Now compute what the year actually produces.

prompts.text: How much does the student deposit over 12 months at $40 a month?
Using the stated rule, how much interest does the account credit for the year?
What is the account worth at the end of the year?
What did the fictional student’s calculation get wrong?
choices: The interest rate; 4% is not the right rate
The base; the rate was applied to one month’s deposit instead of the balance

prompts.text: By how much did the student’s figure understate the year’s interest?
Even at the corrected $9.60, the interest is small. Explain why the student’s conclusion is still wrong, distinguishing what the interest does from what the saving does.

remediation: Use the fictional scenario and work one graded prompt at a time. For each number response, copy the given fictional quantities into integer cents, choose the operation the wording calls for, calculate, and check the result with an inverse operation or estimate. For each choice response, test every option against the stated facts and eliminate an option only when a fact rules it out. For each written response, make a claim and support it with at least one detail from the fictional scenario. Use these steps to check the method while keeping every final result in your own response.
extension: Recompute the year with the account paying 0.4% instead of 4%, and say whether the student’s conclusion becomes right at that rate.
